title: Cheaper AI inference is making it harder to profit from renting out compute
content:
Firm that lets you rent out your idle Mac for AI inference workloads warns of plummeting token costs — Darkbloom network sees earnings drop to $1.23 a day as Anthropic tokens fall 77%
OpenRouter has also started prioritizing speed over cost.
Darkbloom, a decentralized AI inference network that aggregates and sells spare compute capacity from Macs, told its members to expect revenues to fall as token prices continue to drop. According to The Register, the price per million tokens for Anthropic dropped by 77% in under five months, falling to $0.62 in October 2026 from $2.65 in May.
“Data centers have become cheaper. Output per NVIDIA cluster is up ~20x this year, and their margins are wide enough to cut prices 90 percent and still profit at 50 percent,” said Kydo, a researcher from Eigen Labs, the developer of the compute platform. “The market caught up to our price. We could go lower, but then most of you would earn even less [than] nothing.”
It’s estimated that someone running an M5 Pro Mac Mini with 64GB of Unified Memory could earn as much as $192 per month. This is the best-case scenario, though; the median earnings of the top 50 operators on Darkbloom’s leaderboard are about $159.86 per month. This translates to about $5.26 daily or $1,918.50 annually. However, if we account for Anthropic’s 77% token price drop, earnings will fall to a measly $36.77 per month, or about $1.23 per day.
AI token prices are falling so fast that they've even outpaced Moore’s Law, with some reports saying AI is becoming 50% cheaper every quarter and up to 13 times more affordable every year. News of companies blowing through their annual AI budgets in months has less to do with per-token price and more with the number of tokens, as agentic AI use outpaces token price drops. Aside from that, OpenRouter, Darkbloom’s primary client, has started prioritizing decode speed, quantization, and prefill speed, putting users without a top-of-the-line Max or Ultra Apple chip at a disadvantage.
Despite that, Darkbloom says it will not sit idly by and let some users lose out because of these changes. The network is analyzing model demand to advise members on which models are in higher demand right now. It’s also looking at other kinds of workload beyond inference, including distributed CI/CD jobs, improving network performance to better compete against other computer providers/aggregators, and finding other clients outside of OpenRouter.

report.summary: Darkbloom warns idle-Mac compute rentals will earn far less as Anthropic token prices fall 77%, turning a $160 monthly median into about $37.
report.background: Decentralized inference networks like Darkbloom aggregate spare compute from consumer Macs and sell it to AI workloads, promising owners passive income from idle Apple Silicon. That model depends on token prices staying high enough to cover electricity, hardware wear and coordination overhead. But AI inference is commoditizing fast: better serving software, quantized models and massive NVIDIA cluster throughput have pushed output per cluster up roughly 20x, letting data centers cut prices deeply while keeping wide margins. Anthropic's per-million-token price fell from $2.65 in May to $0.62 in October 2026, a 77% drop in under five months. OpenRouter, Darkbloom's main client, is also prioritizing decode speed, prefill speed and quantization, which favors high-end Apple chips and professional operators over casual participants. The result is a squeeze on small, distributed compute suppliers as hyperscale economics reset the market.
key_points: Anthropic's token price dropped 77% in under five months, from $2.65 to $0.62 per million tokens. Darkbloom's median top-50 operator earnings are projected to fall from about $159.86 per month, or $5.26 per day, to roughly $36.77 per month, or $1.23 per day.

Scale economics are crushing small suppliers. An Eigen Labs researcher says NVIDIA cluster output rose about 20x this year, and data centers can cut prices 90% while still earning 50% margins. Darkbloom says it could cut prices further, but most node operators would earn even less than nothing.

Best-case Mac rental income is modest and fragile. An M5 Pro Mac Mini with 64GB unified memory could earn up to $192 per month in ideal conditions, but the median top-50 operator makes about $159.86 monthly. After the token-price collapse, that income no longer justifies treating idle-Mac rental as meaningful passive income.

OpenRouter is now prioritizing decode speed, quantized models and prefill speed, disadvantaging users without top-tier Max or Ultra Apple chips. Darkbloom is responding by analyzing model demand, improving network performance, seeking clients beyond OpenRouter and exploring distributed CI/CD workloads outside pure inference.

The broader trend is deflationary. AI inference costs are falling roughly 50% per quarter, or up to 13x per year, outpacing Moore's Law. Yet agentic AI generates so many tokens that companies still blow annual AI budgets in months, meaning cheaper unit prices do not guarantee lower total spend.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the token-price collapse confirms inference is becoming a commodity, squeezing decentralized and edge compute providers while favoring hyperscalers and highly optimized serving stacks. Developers benefit from cheaper APIs, but must manage total spend as agentic workflows multiply token consumption. Regular users should expect cheaper AI features, but idle-Mac rental schemes look less like passive income and more like a thin-margin hobby. Local Apple Silicon inference remains useful for privacy, offline work and experimentation, not for competing with data-center economics.
report.tools: Watch Darkbloom's demand and earnings dashboards plus OpenRouter's pricing and routing signals. For hands-on testing, try local inference on Apple silicon with MLX and llama.cpp, and compare GPU serving with vLLM or TensorRT-LLM. Track per-token and per-task costs, not just headline prices.
